purpose: This medicine helps treat conditions where your immune system is overactive and causing inflammation, such as rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, plaque psoriasis, and ankylosing spondylitis. It helps reduce pain, swelling, and other symptoms so you can feel better and do more of your daily activities. It is a biosimilar, meaning it works just like the original brand-name drug Humira.
how_it_works: Your immune system makes a protein called TNF-alpha, and in some diseases, the body makes too much of it, which causes harmful inflammation. This medication attaches to that protein and blocks it, like putting a cap on it so it cannot cause damage. By lowering that inflammation, the medicine helps protect your joints, skin, and digestive system from further harm.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include redness, pain, or swelling at the injection site, upper respiratory infections like a cold or stuffy nose, headache, and rash. Some people may also experience nausea or stomach pain.
warnings: This medication lowers your immune system, which means you may get infections more easily, including serious ones like tuberculosis (TB) or fungal infections. Before starting, your doctor will test you for TB. Tell your doctor right away if you develop fever, chills, cough, or feel very unwell. There is also a small increased risk of certain cancers, especially lymphoma. Do not use if you have an active infection. Avoid live vaccines while on this medicine. Contact your doctor before any surgery or vaccinations.
typical_dosing: This medicine is given as an injection under the skin (subcutaneous), usually at home. The dose and how often you take it depends on the condition being treated. For many conditions like rheumatoid arthritis, a common schedule is one injection every other week. Your doctor or nurse will teach you exactly how to inject it and will personalize your dosing schedule for you.
